new_statements.quote: [§3.3.2] Stress does not play a role in the language. Generally there is more stress on higher tones and on nuclear syllables. (For more details see 3.3.3.10.) [§3.3.3.10] Although stress is not significant in the language (see 3.3.2), there seems to be more stress on higher tones and on nuclear syllables. Where these two principles contradict, the following rules may apply: a) When a prefix has a higher tone than the nuclear syllable, the stress is on the prefix (see ex. 38d). b) When a suffix has a higher tone than the nuclear syllable, the stress is on the nuclear syllable (ex. 38g). [§3.5.1] As was stated in 3.3.2, stress is insignificant in the language and basically follows high tones and nuclear syllables.
new_statements.citation: Schaub, Willi. 1985. Babungo. Croom Helm Descriptive Grammars. London: Croom Helm.
new_statements.locator: Ch. 3 Phonology, §3.3.2 'Stress' and §3.3.3.10 'Interaction of tone and stress' (page numbers not recoverable from the search-API snippets; the related §3.5.1 'Stress under morphological processes' straddles pp. 285-286, the running head '286 Phonology' falling inside its second sentence)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Babungo is a tone language (eight lexical pitch types) in which stress is explicitly said to be non-significant / to play no role. Phonetically, prominence falls on the nuclear (root) syllable and on higher-toned syllables; when these conflict, a prefix bearing a higher tone than the root takes the stress, but a higher-toned suffix does not (the root keeps it). An alternative catalog reading is 'no-word-stress-per-source', since the author treats stress as a by-product of tone and root position rather than an independent word-level category.
new_statements.exceptions: A further clause (context truncated in the snippet, apparently where prefix/suffix and root carry the same tone) reads: '... on the nuclear syllable, neither syllable seems to be more stressed than the other.' Stress can also be used, weakly, for constituent emphasis at sentence level (§1.11.2.1.2: 'Stress may be used for constituent emphasis, but this is a weak form...'; elsewhere 'stress is a weak means of expressing emphasis').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (prefix + nuclear syllable + suffix; examples 38a-g are individual words); sentence-level use of stress/loudness for emphasis is treated separately in §1.11.2. Statement is qualitative (no instrumental data).
new_statements.identity_note: Schaub 1985 describes Babungo (= Vengo, veng1238; Wikipedia/Glottolog alternates Ngo, Nge, Vengoo, Pengo), the language of Babungo village on the Ndop Plain, Northwest Region, Cameroon; no dialect distinction is made in the material seen.
